engines_four_underwing:
REAL STANDARD (747-400): EXACTLY FOUR high-bypass turbofans, each on an underwing pylon that slings the nacelle FORWARD of and BELOW the wing leading edge. Inboard pair sits close to the fuselage; outboard pair sits ~two-thirds out the semi-span. Long-duct cowls are fat (fan ~2.4 m dia, roughly 0.37x the fuselage diameter) with a visibly darker, recessed inlet. None on the fuselage, none on the tail, none floating.

THREE.JS TECHNIQUE: Author ONE nacelle as a reusable Group, then clone+mirror it four times — never model four separately. Nacelle = an open-ended CylinderGeometry cowl, capped at the front by a dark near-black ring (TorusGeometry or a slightly smaller inset Cylinder with low-value material) set a few cm INSIDE the lip so the inlet reads open and shadowed, plus a small ConeGeometry exhaust plug at the rear. Pylon = a thin swept BoxGeometry (or tapered wedge) whose top face intersects the wing underside and whose bottom straps over the nacelle crown — overlap both by a small epsilon so it never floats. Build a helper placeEngine(fraction, side) that positions along the wing's swept leading-edge line at semi-span fractions ~0.28 (inboard) and ~0.62 (outboard), offsets each nacelle forward and down of the local leading edge, and mirrors X for the opposite wing. Parent all four to the wing Group so sweep/dihedral carry them automatically. Verify count==4 and that every inlet face normal points into darkness before submitting; this is the highest-weight, currently-weakest criterion, so make the four-ness unmistakable from the given angle.
silhouette_747:
REAL STANDARD: A 747 is read at a glance by THREE simultaneous cues — the partial-length upper-deck hump forward, four underwing engines, and wide-body proportions where overall length (~70.7 m) and wingspan (~64.4 m) are nearly equal, giving a near-square plan bounding box. If any one cue is missing it collapses into a generic airliner; a full-length hump reads as A380, two engines as 767/A330, no hump as 737.

THREE.JS TECHNIQUE: Treat silhouette as an emergent property of correct sub-part proportions, not a thing you model directly. Build the whole aircraft as a parented Group hierarchy (fuselage -> wing -> engines, tail, hump) and lock the master ratios first with named constants: span ~0.9x length, fuselage slenderness ~10.5:1, hump ending at ~1/3 length, engines four. Do a best-of-N pass: render from the given camera angle, then self-check the three cues are each legible in the outline — squint-test the silhouette against 'could this be an A380 or a twinjet?' and fix whichever cue is ambiguous. Keep the four engines and the hump projecting clearly beyond neighboring geometry in the chosen view so they survive as outline features, not just interior detail. Correct proportions + all three cues present = the top band; this criterion is weight 1.4 and currently very weak, so proportion discipline pays the most here.
fuselage_proportions:
REAL STANDARD (747-400): One continuous slender tube — constant-section body ~6.5 m exterior diameter over ~68.6 m length, a slenderness ratio of ~10.5-11:1 (evoking the full ~70.7 m aircraft). A smooth rounded ogive/radome nose tapers in, and the aft fuselage sweeps UP into a long tapering boat-tail cone (APU exhaust at the tip). No segment seams, no steps, no blunt flat ends.

THREE.JS TECHNIQUE: Build the fuselage as a SINGLE revolved mesh to guarantee no seams — define a 2D profile as an array of Vector2 (radius vs. length) that starts at zero at the nose tip, curves up as an ogive, holds constant through the cabin, then tapers back toward the tail, and revolve it with LatheGeometry (radialSegments 48-64 for a smooth round section). One geometry = zero visible joints, and the pointed profile ends give a closed nose/tail with no blunt caps. For the characteristic upswept tail (a lathe is axisymmetric and can't do it alone), post-process the vertices: displace them progressively upward along the rear third as a smooth bend (lerp the offset in by length fraction) — still one BufferGeometry, so no seam appears. Enforce the ~10.5:1 length-to-diameter ratio explicitly with constants; a too-short/fat tube is the classic proportion miss. Keep the cross-section perfectly circular (wide-body double-lobe reads as round from outside).
wing_geometry:
REAL STANDARD (747-400): Low-mounted cantilever wing, quarter-chord sweep 37.5 degrees, 7 degrees dihedral, strongly tapered from a broad root chord to a narrow tip (trailing edge sweeps more than the leading edge), aspect ratio ~7.9, span ~0.9x body length, mounted at the lower-mid fuselage with roots faired smoothly into the belly. The -400 identifier is a 1.8 m canted, highly-swept winglet on each tip.

THREE.JS TECHNIQUE: Model each half-wing as a tapered, swept planform, not a rectangle. Define a Shape with four corner points (root-LE, root-TE, tip-LE, tip-TE) where the tip is offset aft to produce ~37.5 deg leading-edge sweep and the tip chord is much shorter than the root (taper), then ExtrudeGeometry a thin depth for thickness — optionally scale the tip cross-section thinner than the root for spanwise thickness taper. Apply dihedral by ROTATING the whole half-wing Group ~7 deg about the fuselage's roll axis (not by bending vertices). Mount at the lower-mid fuselage and sink the root a few cm INTO the belly, adding a small fillet/faired blend so the wing-body junction isn't a hard butt joint. Mirror the Group for the other side. Add a small canted, swept winglet (another thin extruded trapezoid rotated up ~60-75 deg and swept) at each tip for -400 identity. Span constant ~0.9x length; a stubby or unswept wing is the common failure.
upper_deck_hump:
REAL STANDARD (747-400 with Stretched Upper Deck): The hump begins JUST AFT of the cockpit in the forward fuselage, runs ~15 m (a little over one-third of the body), and blends smoothly (faired) down into the main fuselage crown — never an abrupt step and never full-length (full-length = A380). Critically, the FLIGHT DECK sits LOW: cockpit windows are on the main-deck level, below and forward of the hump, not on top of it. The upper deck carries ~20 windows per side.

THREE.JS TECHNIQUE: Model the hump as a faired lump on the crown, not a stuck-on box. Build it as a half-body: take a stretched half-ellipsoid (a scaled sphere clipped at the belt-line) or loft a spline profile that rises from the crown near the nose, peaks, then tapers back to zero by ~1/3 of the fuselage length. Fair it by overlapping the hump into the fuselage and matching tangents at the trailing blend so the down-slope is gradual (sample the fuselage radius and start the hump surface flush with it). Place the cockpit windshield as small dark angled panels on the NOSE at main-deck height, forward of and below the hump start — getting this low-cockpit relationship right is what separates a real 747 from a generic hump. Add a short row of small upper-deck windows along the hump flank. This criterion is weight 1.5 and currently weak; the two failure modes to avoid are a full-length hump and a cockpit placed atop the hump.
empennage:
REAL STANDARD (747-400): A single VERY TALL swept vertical stabilizer — the fin reaches the aircraft's full ~19.41 m height. Plus a low-mounted pair of swept horizontal stabilizers spanning ~22.2 m with slight dihedral. All surfaces are tapered (broad root chord to narrow tip) and correctly placed on the aft tail cone; both the fin and the tailplane must be present and well-formed.

THREE.JS TECHNIQUE: Reuse the swept-tapered-surface recipe from the wing. Vertical fin = a Shape with a broad root and narrow tip, swept back, ExtrudeGeometry'd thin, mounted vertically on TOP of the aft fuselage and made genuinely tall (proportion its height so the fin tip approaches the overall aircraft height, clearly the tallest point). Horizontal stabilizers = two smaller swept, tapered extruded surfaces, mirrored left/right, mounted LOW on the tail cone (near the base of the fin, not atop it) and rotated a few degrees for dihedral. Sink each root a little into the tail cone and add a small fillet so junctions look faired, not butt-jointed. Parent all three to the fuselage tail so they travel with the upswept boat-tail. Common miss: a fin that's too short/stubby or horizontal stabs that are missing or oversized — keep the fin dominant and the tailplane clearly smaller and swept.
landing_gear:
REAL STANDARD (747-400): A tricycle layout totaling 18 wheels. A single steerable TWO-wheel nose strut forward under the cockpit, plus FOUR main-gear bogies (16 main wheels) — each a four-wheel two-axle truck — arranged in a square footprint: two body-gear bogies retracting into the fuselage belly and two wing-gear bogies at the wing root. Struts have plausible length; no floating wheels, no single central strut.

THREE.JS TECHNIQUE: Only build gear if the given view exposes the underside. Author one wheel as a short CylinderGeometry with its axis rotated to horizontal (thin, fat tire), then a bogie = 4 wheels on 2 axles parented to a small BoxGeometry truck beam. Clone the bogie four times for the mains and place them in the correct square: two under the belly centerline, two outboard at the wing roots. Struts = thin CylinderGeometry/Box legs connecting each bogie up into the belly or wing root — overlap the top of the strut into the body so nothing floats. Nose gear = a shorter strut with a single 2-wheel bogie forward under the cockpit. Enforce the exact counts (nose=2 wheels, each main=4) with a loop, and ground all wheel bottoms to a common y-plane so the aircraft sits level. The classic failures — a lone central gear, a missing bogie, or wheels hovering off their struts — are all count/placement errors, so verify count and contact explicitly.
window_door_lines:
REAL STANDARD (747-400): Clean surface detail — an evenly spaced main-deck passenger window row running the fuselage length, a SEPARATE upper-deck window row on the hump (~20/side), a correctly shaped cockpit windshield on the low nose, and evenly spaced door hints (five main-deck doors per side). These must read as windows/doors, not random specks or one oversized painted band.

THREE.JS TECHNIQUE: Use InstancedMesh for perfectly even spacing — one small dark window quad/box instanced N times along the cabin at constant pitch and constant height on the fuselage flank, positioned by wrapping each instance to the fuselage radius so windows hug the curved surface. Make them small and recessed (a dark, low-emissive material set slightly inboard) so they read as glass, NOT a continuous stripe — even spacing and small size are what the top band rewards. Add a second, shorter instanced row along the hump flank for the upper deck. Cockpit windshield = a few angled dark panels on the nose at main-deck height. Door hints = a handful of slightly larger evenly spaced rectangles at the window line. Mirror the whole set to the other side. Avoid the two failure modes: one giant band (too big) or scattered specks (uneven). If using a texture instead of geometry, keep the window pitch uniform and the row height consistent.
livery_coherence:
REAL STANDARD: An archetypal wide-body scheme — white/light crown and upper fuselage over a grey (or bare-metal light) lower belly and wings, split by a thin colored cheatline stripe at window level running nose-to-tail, consistently colored engine nacelles, and a tasteful accent color on the tall vertical fin. No clashing rainbow parts, no all-black/unlit surfaces, no arbitrary per-part color mismatches.

THREE.JS TECHNIQUE: Assign materials by PART with a small, disciplined palette (2-3 colors + one accent), not random colors per mesh. Upper fuselage = a white MeshStandardMaterial (moderate roughness, low metalness); lower belly and wings = a consistent light grey. Achieve the two-tone split either by modeling upper/lower fuselage as two shells that meet at the window line, or with vertex colors / a material boundary at belt height. Give ALL four nacelles the identical material instance so they match. Put the single accent color on the fin (and optionally a thin cheatline: a slim stripe mesh or a band in the fuselage texture at window level, nose-to-tail). Keep metalness/roughness consistent across the airframe so lighting reads as one aircraft. Ensure every surface is lit (no pure-black unlit faces) and no part carries an off-palette color. Reuse shared material objects so the scheme stays coherent by construction rather than by luck.
craftsmanship:
REAL STANDARD: Clean, deliberate construction — every part joins cleanly with no floating or detached pieces, no holes, no awkward intersecting parts, and no z-fighting/flickering coplanar faces. Junctions (wing-body, engine-pylon-wing, fin-tail, gear-strut) look faired and intentional from the given angle.

THREE.JS TECHNIQUE: Parent everything into a Group hierarchy so mated parts move together and can't drift apart. For every joint, deliberately OVERLAP the two parts by a small epsilon (e.g. sink the wing root into the fuselage, the pylon into both wing and nacelle, struts into the belly) so there are never gaps or floating pieces — but AVOID exactly coincident coplanar faces, which cause z-fighting: offset overlapping surfaces by a few mm or push one slightly inside the other so no two faces are perfectly flush. Use CLOSED geometries (LatheGeometry, capped cylinders, extrudes with caps) so no open ends show as holes. Where surfaces meet, add tiny fillet blends rather than hard butt joints so junctions read as faired. Before submitting, orbit-check (or self-review) from the given angle for: detached parts, visible holes at caps, and flickering faces; merge or reposition offenders. This is weight 1.0 and currently weak, so a clean overlap-not-coincide discipline across every junction is high-value and cheap.
